one_liner: A narrow-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.2x fair value. Interesting below about $228.

profile.what: Chubb is the largest publicly traded property and casualty insurer, covering companies, affluent households and farms in many countries, with a growing life insurance business in Asia.
profile.money: It collects premiums, pays claims and invests the money in between. Profit comes from underwriting, charging more than it pays out, and from investment income on a large bond portfolio.
profile.valued: Insurers are valued on price to book value against their return on equity, and on P/E. Chubb earns a premium for the consistency of its underwriting results.
profile.peer_group: Financials · bank, insurer or asset manager

summary.sentence: A large, disciplined insurer whose results depend on underwriting through the cycle.
strengths: Earnings and book value have risen over the record.
Berkshire Hathaway is a large shareholder.
risks: Balance sheets of insurers are hard to judge from outside.

meaning.what_it_does: The largest publicly traded property and casualty insurer, covering businesses, wealthy households and farms worldwide.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Premiums for insurance, and investment income on the money held before claims are paid.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Disciplined underwriting: it walks away from business priced too cheaply.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: A run of severe catastrophes, or claims costs rising faster than premiums.

moat.summary: A reputation for paying claims and a long record of underwriting profit, in an industry with many competitors.

industry.summary: Insurance changes slowly, but results swing with catastrophes, claims inflation and pricing cycles.

management.summary: Regarded as one of the best underwriters in the industry, with a long record of profitable growth.

valuation.method: Banks are valued on book value, not free cash flow. Justified price-to-book = (ROE − 3% growth) ÷ (required return − 3%), using a normalised ROE of 13.9% (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM, capped at 25%) and a required return of 11% (low) to 9% (high): 1.36–1.81 × book value per share of $205.48.

methods.name: Excess-return model on book value
methods.basis: Book value per share $205.48 × 1.36–1.81. This is how Damodaran values banks and insurers: equity is worth book value plus the returns earned above the cost of equity.
